item.title: Iran Keeps Up Unrelenting Attacks on Ships in the Strait of Hormuz
item.description:
Iran has kept up its unrelenting attacks on ships passing through the Strait of Hormuz, including one this week on a tanker that sustained two hits and left one sailor missing.

So far this month, according to official reports and analysts who track the activity in the region, there have been at least 19 attacks on ships in and near the Strait of Hormuz, a critical waterway that had carried one-fifth of the world’s oil and liquefied natural gas shipments before the United States and Israel attacked Iran in February.

But the assault late Monday night on a disabled tanker has raised new alarms in the shipping industry.

After the vessel, the Tara Gas, was struck once, Iran issued warnings to salvage tugboats providing assistance, said Dimitris Maniatis, the chief executive of Marisks, a maritime risk consultancy. A second attack forced the crew of the Tara Gas to abandon the ship, he said.

The double attack put emergency workers and towing vessels, at risk. Throughout the war, Iran has used attacks to try to force shippers to comply with its claim to control navigation in the strait. Most of the strikes have been single hits that often disable vessels. At least 27 seafarers have been killed and 32 injured, according to official tallies and reporting by The New York Times. At least five sailors are missing.

“The incident may indicate a deliberate effort to extend the effects of an initial attack by discouraging or preventing rescue, recovery and salvage operations,” Mr. Maniatis said. Vessels carrying gas or other hazardous material would be particularly vulnerable.

The Tara Gas, which was carrying liquefied petroleum gas, was struck by an unidentified projectile that caused a fire in the engine room. The vessel issued a distress alert, according to several maritime risk firms.

Initial reports indicated that the crew members were safe.

The next day, however, the vessel was attacked a second time, resulting in a fire, according to the U.K. Maritime Trade Operations Center, which is run by Britain’s Royal Navy.

Of the 25 crew members, all of whom were from India, one was reported missing and two were hospitalized with severe burns, according to Manoj Yadav, who leads the union representing Indian sailors.

The rest of the crew members were evacuated to Khasab, Oman, and search-and-rescue operations were continuing, Mr. Yadav said.

Sarbananda Sonowal, India’s minister of ports, shipping and waterways, said in a post on social media that the Indian government was coordinating with the ship management company and regional rescue authorities to locate the missing sailor.

About two thirds of ships that have been attacked since the start of the war in Iran have sustained only minor damage and were able to continue to their journeys, according to an analysis of U.K. Maritime Trade Operations Center warnings. Most of the rest have been salvaged by vessels that towed them away, though last month two vessels sank. There have been a small number of reported incidents in recent weeks of Iranians targeting salvage vessels.

Martin Kelly, the chief executive officer of Orbital Risk Intelligence, a maritime risk firm, said he believes that Iran’s aim is to stop ships from passing through the strait. He did not think their intention was to harm rescuers, but to ensure that ships could not be salvaged. This raises insurance costs and could serve as a deterrent to shipowners.

“The longer the ship is on fire, the higher the cost of salvage,” he said.

Oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz have picked up considerably since the early months of the war, in large part because the U.S. military has run an extensive operation to shield vessels from Iranian drone and missile attacks. But oil exports through the strait have not fully recovered to prewar levels.

Similarly, global oil prices are higher than they were before the start of the war, though they are down from recent highs. The price of Brent crude, the global benchmark, was around $93 a barrel on Thursday — down more than $20 a barrel since late October — as global supply finally caught up with demand. Even as more oil flows from the Middle East, the higher prices have pushed businesses and consumers to find ways to use less fuel.

The United States has carried out intermittent strikes on Iran, including this week, as peace talks have stalled. Iran has attacked fewer ships this month than in October, the most dangerous month since the start of the war, in which more than 38 attacks took place.

Iran’s neighbors in the Persian Gulf also face heightened threats. Kuwait and Bahrain, an island nation in the Persian Gulf, said on Wednesday that they had intercepted Iranian aerial attacks. The attack on Kuwait, which Iranian state media said had been aimed at U.S. air defense systems and missile launch platforms, was the first Iranian offensive against the country in about two months. Bahrain, which hosts the U.S. Navy’s Fifth Fleet, has reported several attacks since Friday.

Vivian Nereim contributed reporting from Riyadh, Saudi Arabia.

item.title: Russia’s Takeover of Japan Tobacco Units Deals $8.6 Billion Blow
item.description:
Russia has taken over management of Japan Tobacco’s local operations, dealing a multibillion-dollar blow to a cigarette maker one-third owned by the Japanese government, in the latest escalation of President Vladimir Putin’s campaign to seize foreign businesses’ Russian assets.

On Thursday, Japan Tobacco said the seizure would force it to book a loss of roughly $8.6 billion for the Russian business this year, pushing the company into the red for the full year.

Mr. Putin issued decrees two weeks ago placing Japan Tobacco’s Russian subsidiaries under the temporary management of a local company. The move is particularly striking given the Japanese government’s substantial stake in the cigarette maker and underscores the rapid deterioration in relations between Moscow and Tokyo in recent months.

Japan Tobacco, which sells Camel and Winston cigarettes internationally, traces its origins to a national tobacco monopoly established by Japan’s Finance Ministry in 1898. Even after the company went public a century later, the ministry retained a majority stake for more than a decade before gradually reducing its holdings to one-third, the current legally mandated minimum.

Japan has formally protested Russia’s actions, Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama told reporters earlier this month. Japan Tobacco said Thursday that it would “aim to maintain local business operations,” adding that the loss does not mean it planned to sell, relinquish or withdraw from the Russian unit. It said it would take “all available measures” to fulfill responsibilities to stakeholders and protect its rights and assets.

Japan Tobacco has operated in Russia for more than a quarter-century and has become the country’s largest tobacco company by sales volume. Roughly 10 percent of Japan Tobacco’s sales come from the Russian units. It employs roughly 4,000 people there, according to a company spokesman. Its shares have fallen more than 20 percent over the past month.

The seizure is part of a broader push by Mr. Putin to wrest Russian assets from companies based in countries Moscow considers unfriendly. In recent months, he has also targeted the local operations of Swiss food giant Nestlé as well as French and German grocery chains.

Japan joined international sanctions against Russia following its invasion of Ukraine in 2022. But the two countries maintained some economic ties, including through a joint venture in the Sakhalin-2 liquefied natural gas and oil project in Russia’s Far East.

More recently, Mr. Putin has intensified pressure on Japan in what analysts say may be an effort to pressure Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, a foreign policy hawk, while rallying nationalist sentiment at home.

In August, Mr. Putin visited a disputed island seized from Japan at the end of World War II, drawing a rebuke from Ms. Takaichi. Two months later, Russia detained a Japanese journalist, accusing him of gathering intelligence about the country’s military capabilities.

Despite the tensions, Ms. Takaichi and Mr. Putin spoke for about 30 minutes on Wednesday evening at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China. It was the first conversation between the two countries’ leaders since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.

Ms. Takaichi told reporters Thursday that she had raised concerns about “the cases of Japanese nationals being detained and the treatment of Japanese companies.” The two leaders agreed to maintain direct communication, she said, calling that “the biggest progress.”

item.title: Mamdani, Musk, Altman, Lagarde, A.I. and Other DealBook Summit Highlights
item.description:
Andrew here. Wednesday’s DealBook Summit was another huge day of headlines. Thanks to everyone who joined us in person and online. We’ve got all of the highlights below.

In the coming days, we’ll send a special series of newsletters that take you deeper into what was said, and delve into the insights, trends and predictions.

The upside and risk of artificial intelligence. America’s shifting politics and what it means for businesses and global trade. The continued fallout from Jensen Huang’s ouster. These topics and more dominated the discussions on Wednesday at the DealBook Summit.

Over the course of the day, speakers, including Sam Altman of OpenAI and Satya Nadella of Microsoft, dug into the challenges of scaling A.I. and keeping it safe. (Polymarket’s C.E.O., Shayne Coplan, raised eyebrows when he told Andrew that he had A.I. agents trading on his laptop in his green room as he spoke.) Discussions with speakers including Prime Minister Mark Carney of Canada and Mayor Zohran Mamdani of New York touched on their relationships with President Trump before and since Election Day.

Elon Musk surprised many when he described himself as “not MAGA,” and expressed regret for his record-breaking spending spree on Republican candidates after many floundered in the midterm elections.

Watch Andrew’s conversations here and catch up on all of The Times’s coverage here.

Here are some key themes.

Is the recent tech-stock sell-off a blip, or a sign that the A.I. industry is doomed to run out of steam? That was the big question that Christine Lagarde, the president of the European Central Bank, addressed to kick off the event. She warned that while growth in A.I. had helped keep the global economy resilient, it might not end well. There is “a very ambitious price valuation which stands to be corrected eventually,” she said.

On the flip side, Altman, the C.E.O. of OpenAI, an A.I. powerhouse expected to go public as soon as next year, downplayed the “ups and downs of valuations.” Overall, he said, the “trend is going to be strong.”

The debate took on extra emphasis as Anthropic priced a record-setting I.P.O. valuing the giant at more than $1.5 trillion. Its shares are set to begin trading on Thursday.

Beyond the financial fears around how fast the A.I. industry is growing is a fear of how powerful the technology itself has become. Greg Brockman, a founder at OpenAI and its president, said A.I. safety had become a bigger conversation (and focus at his company) as models became more capable.

“Models are now capable enough that we need to think about safety, security, alignment — that’s new,” he said. “And that’s actually been a huge cultural shift.”

Both he and Altman stressed the need for humans to retain tight control over the technology. Nadella of Microsoft, for one, sounded skeptical that so-called alignment — the science of teaching A.I. to broadly follow human preferences and instructions — is fully possible.

Palmer Luckey, a founder of the defense contractor Anduril Industries, sees a potential dark cloud, however. He said he believed that the recent wave of tech outages affecting airlines, banks and our digital lives had an A.I. angle. He blamed tech outages on attackers using A.I. tools to target outdated infrastructure.

“As of right now, there’s a mismatch between the attackers, who are very fast-moving in using technology,” he said, “and old, outdated systems that are not able to adopt technology as quickly as it is developed.”

Mamdani, the mayor of New York City and a democratic socialist, explained a bit about how he maintains an amicable relationship with Trump. He said the key to dealing with the president was “to focus on any possible area of commonality — and the reason for that is the stakes are so immense.”

One example: He said he had called the president to plead his case, asking for a relaxation of regulations to help the city’s bodegas and small retailers meet new federal food-stocking rules.

Carney, the Canadian prime minister, who met with Trump earlier in the day on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China, has found negotiations on the countries’ trade spat progressing slower than he would like. But he also offered a contrasting view. In certain settings, Trump comes across as personable and engaged.

“He listens a lot more in private,” Carney said. “I mean, he’s interested, genuinely, in your opinion, and it’s a reasonably direct conversation.” Even so, Canada is advancing trade ties with China while talks with the Trump administration remain stalled over the tit-for-tat tariff war.

Governance watchdogs have long called into question business figures’ close ties to the president and his family — an issue that could draw serious scrutiny from a Democrat-controlled congress.

David Ellison, the C.E.O. of Skydance, could be one under the political microscope. In conversation with Andrew, Ellison took on issues as big as press freedom and as small as “Rush Hour 4.” Skydance’s decision to greenlight production of that film was for creative and commercial reasons, Ellison said, not because the studio was pressured to do so by Trump, who was previously reported to have requested that the studio revive the franchise.

Ellison’s media conglomerate, Paramount Skydance, was born out of a mega-merger with Warner Bros. after the Justice Department in June shuttered its investigation into the deal. Ellison’s father, Larry Ellison, has a close relationship with Trump.

“We’ve been fortunate enough to be able to work closely with this administration,” Ellison said. But, he added, “when we started the Paramount deal, that was under the Biden administration,” with whom “we were working very closely.”

Later in the day, Coplan of Polymarket defended his company’s ties to Donald Trump Jr., the president’s elder son — who’s an investor in the company via his venture firm 1789 Capital — saying the relationship was “heavily overblown.”

The tech bosses on the agenda — including Altman of OpenAI and Luckey of Anduril — all expressed empathy toward Huang’s predicament after his ouster last week from Nvidia amid reports of his affair with a woman whom U.S. intelligence officials determined to be a Chinese asset.

Some in the Trump administration have suggested Nvidia’s parting with Huang, who has said he would like a shot to return to the chip-making giant, is the right move. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said this week that the company needed a “dramatic shake-up” — widely interpreted as a call for new blood to run Nvidia.

Tech leaders have had kinder words. Altman told Andrew: “I wish Jensen the best. I wish Nvidia the best. I don’t think the world needs another set of random opinions on what’s going to happen here.”

Musk, like others in Silicon Valley, said Huang was irreplaceable.

“Let’s say you’re the Chicago Bulls, middle of your second season, and you’ve got a winning streak that’s just going to happen, and then you kick Michael Jordan off your team,” Musk, the C.E.O. of SpaceX and Tesla, said, adding that this “doesn’t seem like a smart decision to me.”

Anthropic completes its blockbuster I.P.O., lifting tech stocks. The artificial intelligence lab sold $81.3 billion of its stock in the largest ever public listing. Anthropic, the maker of the Claude chatbot, priced its shares at $83, above the preliminary range of $70 to $78, giving the company an initial valuation of about $1.5 trillion. A strong trading debut could alleviate some A.I. bubble fears.

Wall Street’s mega financing for Nvidia reportedly hasn’t been deployed. Investors and Silicon Valley were buzzing over the news this summer that the A.I. bellwether Nvidia had secured $500 billion in pledges from Apollo Global Management, Blackstone and others to help fund some Nvidia customers’ chip purchases. No capital has changed hands so far, however, and now some investors think it will fall short of expectations, The Wall Street Journal reports, citing unnamed sources.

President Trump meets with the leaders of China and Russia. Trump greeted Russia’s president, Vladimir Putin, warmly before a trilateral meeting in Shenzhen, China. A commitment to increase the production and supply of petroleum was among the points agreed to, according to a text of a joint statement released by Russia.

The Fed weighs more interest rate increases. Central bank officials predicted at their meeting last month that they would need to raise the Fed’s benchmark lending rate to combat inflation. The futures market on Thursday was signaling three rate increases over the next year.

Christine Lagarde: “The rest of the world is looking at the United States thinking institutions can actually hold — in spite of whatever happens.”

The departing president of the European Central Bank said that there were signs that democracy was alive and well in the United States again, in a much more positive assessment than she had earlier this year, when she described the country as acting strangely and undermining trust with its allies.

Mark Carney: “It should have been done six months ago, but we’re not going to sign something that doesn’t make sense for Canada.”

The prime minister of Canada commented on the recently revived trade talks between his country and the United States. While Washington has backed off on some minor issues, there’s no sign of a breakthrough on critical issues including the tariffs of up to 50 percent on Canadian steel, auto and aluminum exports.

Hailey Bieber: “It can be distorting to the mind, especially those filters that change your face — they make your lips bigger, your nose smaller.”

Bieber has used social media — where she has nearly 60 million Instagram followers and almost 20 million on TikTok — to great success with her beauty brand, Rhode, which was sold last year for at least $800 million. But she is also fully aware of the perils of the technology, which can be addictive and can make her feel insecure. “But it’s part of the world we’re living in — it’s not going anywhere,” she added.

Palmer Luckey: “Everyone already knows we need more killer robots.”

Luckey, a founder of the defense tech company Anduril Industries, said that his role in discussions with the military and the government about the future of war was to point out things that they may not have considered. As new as autonomous warfare may seem to many, killer robots are old news to Luckey and to many steeped in defense at this point. What Luckey tries to do is suggest ideas that people in the public sector may not have considered, such as how tech might be used to control the weather in the context of war.

Vlad Tenev: “I don’t want to be the one telling you that you can’t trade something.”

Tenev, the C.E.O. of Robinhood — speaking alongside the Nasdaq chief Adena Friedman and the Polymarket founder Shayne Coplan — weighed in on a debate about the blurry line between investing and gambling. He argued that regular traders should have access to the same investment opportunities available to the ultrawealthy.

Sam Altman: “We’re not going to be able to make everybody happy.”

OpenAI’s C.E.O. appeared with the company’s president, Greg Brockman, and discussed how OpenAI had to balance addressing artificial intelligence safety issues with continuing progress on A.I. development. And while its rival Anthropic is set to begin trading on Thursday, OpenAI’s I.P.O. future is thought to be in the cards next year. Altman said on Wednesday that the public listing would come “at some point.”

Satya Nadella: Founders are “singular, but they’re not gods.”

Microsoft’s C.E.O. said that he had confidence in the leaders of Nvidia and that the company could still succeed without its co-founder, Jensen Huang, at the helm. Founders are incredible, he said, because they have created something out of nothing. But he made the case that founders should be proud when their companies thrive beyond their tenure; otherwise, what did they build?

Zohran Mamdani: “Comrades. It’s great to be here at the largest D.S.A. meeting Lincoln Center has ever seen.”

The mayor of New York City calls the local chapter of the Democratic Socialists of America his political home, but he is also famously amiable and eager to present himself as willing to engage with people from across the political spectrum, including President Trump. On Wednesday, the first words he uttered were clearly meant to disarm the crowd, many of whom chuckled in response.

David Ellison: “If there was any opportunity to be able to collaborate with him in the future, from our perspective, it would be a privilege.”Ellison discussed Elon Musk’s investment in Paramount. He left the door open to future collaboration with Musk amid speculation that Starlink might offer Paramount content on its service, which is used by a number of airlines.

Elon Musk: “I’m not MAGA”The billionaire, who gave nearly $500 million to back Republican candidates in the midterm elections, sought to play down his ties to the party after a drubbing at the polls. Musk said he felt “pretty foolish” about spending so much “and not seeing much for it.” There are “positives and negatives in both” political parties, he added.

item.title: Here’s the latest.
item.description:
Anthropic, the artificial intelligence giant, will begin trading on the stock market later Thursday, a bellwether debut for a major A.I. company amid a global technology race and boom some have cautioned could become a bubble.

The company completed its initial public offering as the world’s largest stock market debut, a testament to investors’ belief in the A.I. giant’s business prowess, valuing the company at more than $1.5 trillion. Anthropic’s shares will begin trading on Thursday on Nasdaq under the symbol ANT.

Anthropic’s offering is the first time that public market investors will have the chance to invest in one of the A.I. industry’s “frontier labs,” which are developing the core models underlying the boom. The company’s offering prospectus showed a fast-growing business alongside a narrative of future growth and abundance, including curing diseases and expanding economic prosperity. Revenue soared to $33 billion in the first nine months of the year from $41 million in 2023.

The company could also pave the way for other enormous debuts, including by OpenAI, which has filed for an I.P.O. and may go public next year.

Here’s what else to know:

Initial public offering: Anthropic confirmed on Wednesday that its I.P.O. price was set at $83 a share and that it had sold more than 980 million shares, including some from its founders, for $81.3 billion. The company also planned to raise $26 billion through a private placement, bringing its total haul from the offering to $107 billion. The company’s offering topped that of Elon Musk’s SpaceX, which in June raised a then record-breaking $75 billion at a higher valuation: $1.77 trillion. Read more ›

Power play: Anthropic is going public partly because its voracious demand for computing power is hugely expensive. The company has issued convertible debt to finance some of the infrastructure it needs, like chips, data centers and electricity. But this debt, which turns into equity in the future, is counted as a loss on Anthropic’s books, resulting in a net loss of $104 billion so far this year. Read more ›

Nvidia’s shadow: Anthropic’s public offering is set to the backdrop of turmoil at the chip maker Nvidia, whose chief executive, Jensen Huang, resigned last week. Read more about Mr. Huang’s downfall, and the blockbuster earnings his company reported on Tuesday ›

Knives out: Dario Amodei, the chief executive of Anthropic, has for years exasperated his peers with warnings about extreme risks of A.I., even as his company has built some of the most powerful A.I. systems in the world. For some of his peers in Silicon Valley, frustration has turned to hostility. Read more ›

Corporate structure: Anthropic is set to become by far the largest publicly traded “public benefit corporation.” The unusual governing structure mandates the company balance safety and profit, creating a vast “experiment” in corporate power. Read more ›

item.title: When will Anthropic shares start trading?
item.description:
The U.S. stock market opens at 9:30 a.m. Eastern, but don’t expect shares of Anthropic to begin trading right away.

Delaying the start of trading in shares in a newly public company is part of an elaborate effort to ensure that the stock’s introduction into the market goes as smoothly as possible.

A key part of that is deciding at what price Anthropic should begin trading.

Bankers will spend Thursday morning trying to assess from traders how much demand there is to sell and buy Anthropic shares at various prices. They are looking for an “equilibrium” price: the price at which there is generally the same amount of sellers as buyers.

The goal is to make sure that the company’s shares are relatively stable when they begin to trade. Ideally, underwriters hope they will rise gradually throughout the trading day. Ultimately, the price bankers land on for the opening trade could be below, above or the same as the $83-a-share initial public offering price that was determined on Wednesday night.

For such a large offering as Anthropic, it could take hours for the process to play out before the trading can start.

Several previous high-profile listings were in the late morning: Shares of Alibaba, the Chinese e-commerce giant, began trading at 11:53 a.m. on Sept. 19, 2014; and shares of Twitter began trading a little before 11 a.m. on Nov. 7, 2013. Shares of SpaceX started trading just before noon on June 12.

item.title: How Anthropic’s Dario Amodei thinks about A.I.
item.description:
Even before he earned his doctorate in physics from Princeton two decades ago, Dario Amodei had made a habit of soaking up information about artificial intelligence, its prospects, its risks and its responsibility to humanity.

He became absorbed in obscure blogs where writers discussed A.I.’s potential to wipe out humanity. He delved into the online forums where intellectuals debated how to make the most money for philanthropy.

One night in 2007, he regaled a friend with his thoughts on a book that predicted that artificial intelligence would eventually surpass the human brain — a milestone that Dr. Amodei told his friend could happen within their lifetimes.

These books, blogs and online communities have influenced Dr. Amodei to this day, according to interviews with more than two dozen of his classmates, friends, teachers and colleagues. They help explain the ideas that drive the 43-year-old chief executive of Anthropic, a company that is set to conduct one of the world’s largest public listings this month, and offer an understanding of how the man at the forefront of the A.I. revolution actually thinks about A.I.

item.title: China Is Shut Out of a Blockbuster Public Offering Once Again
item.description:
It was the biggest initial public offering in history and investors from China and Hong Kong were left out.

Anthropic, the artificial intelligence company and maker of the Claude chatbot, excluded investment from Chinese and Hong Kong firms from buying its shares in advance of the I.P.O., according to three people with knowledge of the decision, who asked not to be identified because they were not authorized to speak publicly.

A representative for Anthropic declined to comment, and the reason for not accepting investments from the region was not clear. But it follows a move by the Trump administration to keep artificial intelligence out of China’s reach. Both Washington and Beijing are drawing red lines around their homegrown technology as they compete for supremacy in A.I.

It also follows a similar move by SpaceX and its bankers to shut out China from its blockbuster public offering in July. OpenAI, another leading A.I. company, is expected to bar Chinese investors from its eventual public offering. OpenAI has already barred Chinese investors from participating in private fund-raising. All three companies have counted the U.S. government as a client.

The news that Anthropic would bar Chinese investors was reported earlier by Bloomberg.

President Trump and China’s leader, Xi Jinping, met on Thursday at the APEC meeting in the Chinese city of Shenzhen, where Mr. Xi called on members to build an “open ecosystem” for technology.

Both Mr. Trump and Mr. Xi are trying to inject some stability — and a little bonhomie — into an increasingly rocky economic relationship between the world’s two biggest economies. But their governments continue to build fortresses around trade, technology and capital.

Hours before Mr. Trump arrived in Asia to attend meetings with regional leaders, his administration moved to restrict China’s access to advanced artificial intelligence chips. In response, China warned it could hit back, saying “if the U.S. persists, China will take countermeasures.”

“China is deeply concerned about — and firmly opposes — a series of recent economic and trade restrictive measures taken by the U.S. against China,” a spokesman for China’s Ministry of Commerce said on Thursday.

China experts warned that the new A.I. rule, the latest in a series of escalatory moves from both sides, will make it harder for both Mr. Xi and Mr. Trump to come to any meaningful agreement to de-escalate rising conflict between the world’s biggest economies.

“At a minimum this step — and potential others yet to come — complicate reaching a deal to extend the cease-fire,” said Scott Kennedy, researcher at the Center for Strategic and International Studies in Washington.

item.title: Meet Anthropic’s seven founders. Each is now worth about $20 billion.
item.description:
Anthropic’s seven founders created the company in 2021 after leaving OpenAI in a dispute over how artificial intelligence should be built. Now each holds a stake worth about $20 billion as Anthropic goes public.

They include Dario Amodei, 43, the chief executive who published a 3,800-word essay in September calling for a global slowdown of A.I. development, and his younger sister Daniela Amodei, who manages Anthropic’s business operations and the company’s executive leadership.

Jared Kaplan, Anthropic’s chief science officer, met Dario Amodei in the mid-2000s while car-pooling to an event for a fellowship both received in graduate school. Jack Clark, the company’s head of public benefit, leads the Anthropic Institute, an internal think tank focused on A.I.’s societal, economic and security impacts.

“None of us wanted to found a company,” the company’s chief architect, Sam McCandlish, said in a round-table discussion with the other founders posted on Anthropic’s YouTube channel in 2024. “We just felt like it was our duty.”

Tom Brown, Anthropic’s chief compute officer, once worked at OpenAI, where he was one of the company’s first 20 employees. Christopher Olah, who at 34 is the youngest of the seven Anthropic founders, used a speech at the Vatican in May to urge the world to scrutinize A.I. development and “tell the labs when we are failing.”
